title: Pointer Arithmetic
concept: Pointer addition moves to the 'next space' (not incrementing by 1!)

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
Header for using `printf`.

The key point of this lesson is that when you add 1 to a pointer, the address moves by `sizeof(type)`, not 1.

steps.title: main function definition
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created and the array `arr` and pointer `p` are prepared.

The pointer `p` points to the array elements in order and reads their values.

steps.title: array declaration
steps.explanation:
Array `arr` stores 10, 20, 30 in contiguous memory.

This continuity allows pointer addition to find the exact location of the next element.

steps.title: Initialize the pointer to the start of the array
steps.explanation:
In `int *p = arr;`, `arr` decays to `&arr[0]` and is stored in `p`.

That is, `p` becomes the starting pointer pointing to the first element.

steps.title: Pointer dereference
steps.explanation:
`*p` reads the value of the element currently pointed to by `p`.

At startup it points to the first element, so the result is the value `arr[0]`.

steps.title: Pointer arithmetic 1: p + 1
steps.explanation:
`p + 1` moves to the next element address. The actual amount of movement is `sizeof(int)`.

So `*(p+1)` is equal to the value of the second element.

steps.title: Pointer arithmetic 2: p + 2
steps.explanation:
In the same way, `*(p+2)` reads the third element.

To summarize, `*(p+n)` works the same as `arr[n]`.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
Exit with `return 0;`.

The key formula is `p+n -> p + n*sizeof(type)`.

quiz.question: int *p = 1000; When , what is the value of p + 2? (int is 4 bytes)

misconceptions.why:
`*p + 1` means (*p value) + 1, that is, adding 1 to the value, and `*(p+1)` reads the value of the next address.
Parentheses are life.

keyTakeaway: If you add 1 to the pointer, the memory address increases by `sizeof(type)`. (Jump to the next space)
